idiom_name: std::function<void(const Message&)> registered on a channel
implementation_notes: The endpoint collapses into one type-erased callable per (channel, service) pair: register a std::function<void(const Message&)> on the subscription and let the lambda extract the payload, call the service and publish the result. std::function is a polymorphic wrapper that stores lambdas, function objects and member-function pointers alike, so no endpoint class hierarchy is needed. The classic structure (an interface plus one class per service) is still justified when a single endpoint must dispatch to many services selected at run time from the message, e.g. through a registry keyed by message type.
pitfalls: Capturing this in a lambda registered on a long-lived channel leaves a dangling reference once the owner is destroyed; capture by value or use shared_from_this().
std::function copies the closure, so state mutated through a by-value capture is lost after the call; reach the service through a reference, pointer or std::ref.
An exception escaping the handler into the messaging library's dispatch thread is not translated into an error channel and usually terminates the process.

variants.name: C++20 coroutine activator (co_await receive / invoke / send)
variants.idiom_name: awaitable activator coroutine over the channel and the service
variants.implementation_notes: With C++20 coroutines the endpoint becomes a coroutine that co_awaits the next message, co_awaits the service and co_awaits the reply send, so the dispatch chain reads as straight-line code while the completion handlers are generated by the compiler; the coroutine state is heap-allocated and holds everything needed to resume. Choose it when the toolchain is C++20 and callback nesting obscures the error path; the std::function form remains preferable for tiny handlers and for code bases pinned to C++11/14/17.
pitfalls: A coroutine frame outlives the scope that started it: the channel, the service and every captured reference must stay alive for the whole loop, or the resume after co_await touches freed memory.
An exception that escapes an awaitable without an error-translating wrapper never reaches the error channel; it ends on the runtime's unhandled-exception path.
co_await without an executor to resume on turns the loop into a hand-written scheduler; the runtime's event loop must own the resumption.
